### What is the book of 2 Chronicles about?

The book of 2 Chronicles is the second part of a history of David and his descendants who were kings of Israel (Yisrael) and Judah (Yehudah). The first part, the book of 1 Chronicles, ends with the death of David. This book describes David’s successors up to the time of the Babylonian exile. (The books of Ezra and Nehemiah (Nehemyah) continue this story further and tell what happened after the Israelites (Israelis) returned from exile.)

This entire history was compiled and composed after the Judeans (Yehudim) returned from exile in Babylon (Bavel). It is designed to show the restored community that it can still fulfill the purposes that Yahweh has for it as his chosen people. It shows how various Judean (Yehudi) kings, after periods of unfaithfulness to Yahweh when the kingdom declined, restored the true worship of Yahweh and renewed the kingdom’s strength and prosperity.

The message is one of encouragement for the returned exiles. It may have been difficult for them to think of themselves as a distinctive community. They were still ruled by a foreign emperor, and their cities and their temple were in ruins. But the book stresses that if they will worship Yahweh in the way that he desires, particularly following the arrangements that David established, not only will this restore their special identity, their renewed community life will also help people from all nations come to have faith in Yahweh.

### Who wrote the book of 2 Chronicles?

The author of 2 Chronicles does not state his name, and he does not provide any personal information about himself. So it is not possible to identify who wrote this book.

### What title should translators use for this book?

Translators can use a traditional title such as “The Second Book of Chronicles” or “Second Chronicles.” They might also call it by a different title such as “The Successors of King David.”

### What kind of writing is the book of 2 Chronicles?

The book of 2 Chronicles consists essentially of historical narratives, that is, stories about things that happened in the past. Think about how people tell stories in your culture and how you can translate this book in such a way that your readers will recognize that it is telling stories.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### The role of the king

The book of 2 Chronicles focuses on the lives of various kings. Their role was more than just political. The king in ancient Israel (Yisrael) was seen as Yahweh’s appointed representative, entrusted with the task of leading the people to obey the covenant Yahweh had made with them. His success or failure was directly tied to his faithfulness to God. The king was responsible for upholding justice, protecting vulnerable people, and ensuring that the Israelites (Israelis) remained faithful to Yahweh as their God. When the king sinned or worshiped other gods, the entire nation suffered the consequences, because the king was no longer leading the people to live in the way that Yahweh wants people to live.

### The centrality of the temple

A major theme in 2 Chronicles is that Yahweh’s temple in Jerusalem (Yerushalem) was to be the central place of worship for the Israelites, rather than the “high places” where the Canaanites (Kena’anim) had previously worshiped their foreign gods. The book describes in detail how King Solomon (Shelomoh) had his workers construct this temple as a place where Yahweh would be recognized as especially present. The temple served as the primary location for sacrifices, prayers, and festivals. It symbolized the covenant relationship between Yahweh and the Israelites. The dedication of the temple marked a high point in Israel’s history. Its subsequent neglect and the establishment of rival places of worship by unfaithful kings directly led to the nation’s spiritual decline.

### The significance of prophets

Throughout 2 Chronicles, Yahweh speaks to the Israelites through prophets who serve as his messengers. Prophets such as Shemaiah (Shemayah), Oded, Micaiah (Mikayah), Elijah (Eliyah), and Isaiah (Yeshayah) spoke truth to powerful leaders held them accountable for their actions. The prophets often challenged the king’s actions when they conflicted with God’s law. They confronted the idolatry and worship of foreign gods that plagued the kingdom. The prophets’ words and deeds served as a powerful reminder that Yahweh’s power and authority were greater than those of any human ruler, and so it was vital for the king and people to live in a faithful and obedient covenant relationship with Yahweh.

## Part 3: Translation Issues in This Book

### Translating names

This book presents many names of people and places. We recommend that in your translation, you spell them the way they sound in your language. However, if a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the spelling that it uses for some common names if that would be more familiar to your readers. For example, a translation in your region might use the name “Solomon,” and you may choose to use that name rather than spelling it “Shelomoh.”

In many cases, the text indicates whether a person is a man (by identifying him as someone’s father, son, or brother) or a woman (by identifying her as someone’s mother, daughter, sister, or wife). Notes will say when a person is a woman if this is not indicated in the text. Otherwise, translators may assume that the person is a man.

In the same way, the text will typically indicate whether a place name is for a city (“Upper Beth Horon and Lower Beth Horon, cities of fortification,” 8:5), a region (“the land of Edom,” 8:17), a mountain (“Mount Moriah (Moriyah),” 3:1), a waterway (“the wadi of Kidron,” 15:16), and so forth. If your language has its own way of expressing the names of particular kinds of places, you should be able to follow these indications to know how to represent such names.

### “And it happened”

The author often uses the phrase “And it happened” to introduce a new event in the story or a new development within an event. For example, in 7:11, he introduces the development of the cloud of Yahweh’s glory filling the temple at Solomon’s (Shelomoh’s) dedication ceremony by saying, “And it happened, when the priests came out from the holy place.” To translate this phrase in its various occurrences, use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event or development.

### “And now”

“And now” was an expression that speakers and writers in this culture commonly used to introduce their main topic. For example, in 2:7, Solomon uses it to introduce the main point of his letter to King Hiram, which is to request a master craftsman and timber. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language.

### “behold”

The author and characters often use the word “behold” to focus their listeners’ attention on what they are about to say. While the word literally means “look,” the speakers do not want their listeners to look at something, but to pay careful attention. For example, in 11:4 to call King Hiram’s attention to his plan to build a temple for Yahweh.

### “brothers”

The author and characters often use the term “brothers” to mean not sons of the same father but members of the same nation, tribe, clan, or extended family. For example, For example, in 11:4, a prophet tells the Judeans (Yehudim) “you shall not fight with your brothers.” He means the northern tribes of Israel (Yisrael), their fellow descendants of Abraham (Avraham) and members of their same nation.

### “to this day”

In 2 Chronicles 5:9, 8:8, 10:19, and 21:10, the author uses the phrase “to this day.” He uses the comparable expression “to today” in 35:25. He is drawing on earlier sources that are referring to the time when they were written. Translators should be aware that “to this day” refers to a time that was already in the past when 2 Chronicles was written centuries ago. They must avoid giving the impression that the expression refers to the present day of their own readers. Notes at each instance will suggest how a translation might express the meaning accurately.

### “in the eyes of”

The author and characters often speak of something being good or bad, or right or wrong, “in the eyes of” someone. For example, the author says in 14:2 that “Asa did the good and the right in the eyes of Yahweh his God.” He means that Asa did things that were good and right from Yahweh’s perspective or in his judgment.

### “to the face of”

The expression “to the face of” can have different shades of meaning, depending on the context.
* The author and characters often use the word “face” to represent the presence of a person or group, by association with the way people can see the face of someone who is present. For example, the author says in 1:6 that Solomon (Shelomoh) offered sacrifices “to the face of Yahweh.” He means that he did so in the presence of Yahweh.
* The focus may also be on something being in front of or before a person or thing, in space or in time. For example, the author says in 1:5 that the altar of bronze was “to the face of” the tent of meeting. He means that it was in front of it. In 1:12, Yahweh speaks to Solomon of the kings who were “to your face.” He means the kings who ruled various kingdoms before him.
* Sometimes the idea of “in front of” has a further association. For example, the author says in 19:16 that when the Arameans gathered a large army, “Shophach (Shofak), the commander of the army of Hadadezer, was to their faces.” By saying that Shophach was in front of these troops, he means that he was commanding them.
* The focus may also be on the relationship or interaction between people or groups, as in 12:5, where the author relates that Judean (Yehudi) leaders took refuge in Jerusalem (Yerushalem) “from the face of Shishak.” He means that fled from Shishak as his Egyptian (Mitsri) army advanced to attack them.

In other contexts, the author or a character may use the word “face,” describing part of a person, in order to represent that whole person. For example, in 10:2, the author says that Jeroboam (Yarov’am) fled to Egypt (Mitsrayim) “from the face of Solomon.” He is using one part of Solomon, his “face,” to mean all of him in the act of trying to kill Jeroboam. He means that Jeroboam fled from Solomon himself.

### “into the hand of” or “into your hand”

The author and characters often use the word “hand” to represent a person’s power, capability, control, or activity. For example, Solomon says 6:4 that Yahweh has “fulfilled by his hand” what he “spoke by his mouth.” He is saying that Yahweh kept his promise to David by his own power and activity.

The word “hand” may also represent possession or conveyance. The author says in 30:16 that at Hezekiah’s (Hizkiyah’s) Passover celebration, “The priests were sprinkling the blood from the hand of the Levites.” He means that the Levites were conveying this blood from the sacrifices to the priests. (They were doing that in bowls, not literally in their hands.) The word “hand” may also represent agency. The author says in 1:17 of Solomon’s (Shelomoh’s) traders that he exported horses and chariots “by their hand,” that is, through their agency. Notes will help distinguish the difference between these shades of meaning when that may not be clear from the context.

In other contexts, the author or a character may use the word “hand,” describing part of a person, in order to represent the whole person. The author speaks in 30:6 of letters that came “from the hand of the king and his princes.” He is using one part of them, their hands, to mean all of him in the act of writing these letters.

### “head”

The author and characters often use the term “head” to mean “leader.” In 13:12, King Abijah (Aviyah) of Judah (Yehudah) tells King Jereboam of Israel (Yisrael) that he should not fight against him because he cannot win, since “with us at the head is God.” Abijah means that God, not he, is actually leading and commanding the Judean (Yehudi) army.

### “house” meaning “temple”

The author and characters often speak of the temple in Jerusalem (Yerushalem) as if it were a “house” in which Yahweh lived. The idea is that Yahweh is present in a special way in his temple. For example, the author says in 2:1 that Solomon wanted to build a “house” for Yahweh. He means that Solomon wanted to build a temple for him.

### “house of fathers”

In many places, the author uses the phrase “house of fathers” (or “father’s house”) as a common expression of his culture to describe extended families, comprising three or four generations, led by a man who was the father, grandfather, or great-grandfather of the family members. The household also included servants. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, throughout the book you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning (such as “clans”), or you could state the meaning plainly (as by saying “extended families”).

### “let” and “may”

The ULT uses the English helping verbs “let” and “may” to show that a speaker is expressing a desire that something happen or that someone do something. It uses the verb “let” for more assertive expressions, and it uses the verb “may” for more deferential expressions.
For example, the prophet Oded encourages the Judeans (Yehudim) by saying “let your hands not slacken.” He means “you must not let your hands slacken” or “you must not be afraid.” He is being assertive because he is speaking on behalf of Yahweh. Languages that do not have a volitional form might use an imperative form and say “do not let your hands slacken.”
 When Solomon (Shelomoh) says to Yahweh in 1:9, “may your word with David my father be confirmed,” he is saying what he wants Yahweh to do, but he is being more deferential, because he is addressing a superior. Languages that do not have a volitional form might say, “I desire that you confirm what you said to David my father,” or they might use an imperative with an indication that it is a polite request, “may your word with David my father please be confirmed.” Translate this volitional form in the most natural way in your language to indicate that the speaker is expressing what he wishes someone would do.

### “listen” and “hear”

The author and characters may use the terms “listen” or “hear” to mean complying with what someone has said. For example, in 6:19 Solomon asks Yahweh to “listen” to his prayer. He means that he wants Yahweh to answer his prayer by doing what he has requested.

### name of a person representing him and associated or accompanying people

The author and characters often use the name of a person to represent that person and others who are associated with or accompanying that person. For example, in 2:2, when the author says that Solomon numbered the foreigners in Israel (Yisrael), he is using Solomon, one person who was involved in this action, to represent everyone who was involved. The text makes clear that Solomon actually had his officials do this.

### name of nation, tribe, or city representing its people

The author and characters often use the name of a nation, tribe, or city to represent its people or its army. For example, in 2:7, when the author describes Achar (Akar) as “the troubler of Israel,” he is using the name of the nation of Israel to mean the people of that nation, the Israelites (Israelis). (When a nation has the same name as its ancestor, as in this case, this is the same thing as using the name of the ancestor to mean his descendants.)

### “saying”

The author and characters frequently use the term “saying” to introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

### “shall”

The ULT represents the Hebrew instructional verb form with the English helping verb “shall.” For example, when Yahweh asks Solomon (Shelomoh) in 1:7, “What shall I give you?” he means “Tell me what I should give you.” Translate this form with the most natural way in your language for giving instructions.

### “sons of”

The author and characters often speak of “the sons of” a person to mean the nation or tribe that consists of his descendants. For example, the author refers in 5:2 to the “sons of Israel (Yisrael).” In such contexts, “sons” does not mean first-generation offspring, but later descendants. The author is referring to the Israelites (Israelis) as a nation.

### “strike/struck”

In many places, the author says that soldiers “struck” an opposing army, city, or king as if they had merely hit them. But he means that they attacked those opponents and usually that they defeated them. In 16:4, when the author says that Ben Hadad’s army “struck” certain cities in Israel, he means that it attacked them. In 6:24, where Solomon prays about the possibility that the Israelite (Israeli) army may be “struck” by an enemy. He means an enemy may defeat them. In some contexts, the specific meaning of “struck” is “killed.” The author says in 25:3 that Amaziah (Amatsyah) “struck” the officials who had “struck” his father Joash (Yoash). He means that those officials had killed Joash and that to punish them, Amaziah killed them. Another use of the term “struck” is to mean “afflicted with an illness,” as in 21:18.

### travel descriptions marked for change in elevation (“went up,” “went down”)

In Hebrew, writers and speakers generally indicated whether people were going up to a higher elevation or going down to a lower elevation when they traveled. For example, in 1:17, the author says that Solomon’s (Shelomoh’s) traders “brought up” chariots from Egypt (Mitsrayim). He says “brought up” because Jerusalem (Yerushalem), where the traders brought these chariots, was higher than Egypt. If your language does not generally mark travel for change in elevation, you do not need to do that in your translation.

### “walking” representing “living”

The author and characters often speak of how a person lives as if that were a way or path that the person was walking along. For example, in 6:16, Solomon reminds Yahweh of his promise to David that his descendants would also rule Israel (Yisrael) if they would “walk” in his “law.” Solomon means that these descendants would obey Yahweh’s law and live as he wants people to live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly in such cases.

# 2 Chronicles 1 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this book, the author continues the history he began in 1 Chronicles of David and his descendants who were kings of Israel (Yisrael) and Judah (Yehudah). That book ends with the death of David. In this book, the author describes David’s successors up to the time of the Babylonian exile. He begins in chapters 1–9 with an account of the reign of David’s son Solomon (Shelomoh).

1. Introduction to the reign of Solomon (1)
2. Solomon and the Israelite (Israeli) leaders go to worship Yahweh (2–6)
3. Solomon asks Yahweh for wisdom (7–12)
4. The prosperity of Solomon’s kingdom (13–17)

# 2 Chronicles 2 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of Solomon (Shelomoh). It describes the preparations he made to build a temple for Yahweh and a royal palace for himself. It tells how he arranged with Hiram, the king of the nearby city of Tyre (Tsor), to provide him with the timber he needed and how he organized a workforce of resident foreigners to carry loads and quarry large stones.

1. Introduction (1)
2. Solomon’s workforce (2)
3. Solomon writes to Hiram (3–10)
4. Hiram responds to Solomon (11–16)
5. Solomon’s workforce (17–18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why does the author describe the size of Solomon’s workforce twice?

In both 2:2 and 2:18, the author records that Solomon (Shelomoh) had 70,000 burden bearers, 80,000 stone quarriers, and 3,600 overseers. This is not redundancy or unnecessary repetition. The statement in verse 2 is a summary introduction to the events that this chapter describes. It anticipates their outcome. Solomon first had to arrange with Hiram to send him timber, then he needed to arrange for a workforce to transport the timber. The statement in verse 18 concludes the chapter by reporting the end of this process. Putting similar statements at the start and end of an account is a literary technique that was characteristic of Hebrew storytelling. We recommend that you translate both of these statements in the same way so that your readers can appreciate that the author is using this technique.

### When did David count the foreigners in Israel (Yisrael)?

In 2:17, the author describes how Solomon counted the foreign men in Israel in order to organize a workforce to help build the temple. He says that this was “after the numbering in which David his father had numbered them.” There is not a specific record in the historical books of the Bible of David doing this. However, 1 Chronicles 22:2 reports, “And David said to gather the foreigners who were in the land of Israel. And he appointed cutters to cut out stones of hewing to build the house of God.” We may infer from this that David had his officials take a census of the foreigners at this time when they were gathered together.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Was the master craftsman of the palace named Huram or Hiram?

In 2:13, King Hiram tells Solomon that he is sending him a man named Huram Abi (Avi) to make all of the bronze articles for the temple. In [1 Kings 7:13](../1ki/07/13.md), however, this man’s name is spelled “Hiram.” To make clear that this is the same person, some versions use the name Hiram here in 2 Chronicles as well. However, we do not recommend that you change the name either here or in 1 Kings to make the accounts in both books match. The difference in spelling may reflect how Hebrew pronunciation changed during the time between the writing of 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles. So we recommend that you simply translate the names as they appear in each text and not try to harmonize them.

# 2 Chronicles 3 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s description of how Solomon (Shelomoh) built a temple for Yahweh. It describes the dimensions, design, and decorations of the temple.

1. Location and date of the temple construction (1–2)
2. Dimensions of the temple (3–4a, 8a)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “cubit”

Throughout this chapter, the author gives distance measurements in “cubits.” These cubits were ordinarily a unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 46 centimeters or about 18 inches. However, the author specifies that this was the “former measure,” that is, the long or royal cubit, which was a handbreadth longer, or another 10 centimeters or 4 inches. If it would be helpful to your readers, throughout this chapter you could express these lengths in modern measurements, either in the text of your translation or in a footnote. The UST models one way to do that.

### The name of a person representing that person and associated or accompanying people

Throughout this chapter, the author uses Solomon (Shelomoh) to represent the many workers who were involved in constructing the temple. For example, he says of Solomon in verse 5 that “he covered the great house with wood of cypress.” He means that Solomon’s workers did this. In verses 15–17, the author begins to describe the many things that Huram Abi (Avi), the man whom King Hiram of Tyre (Tsor) sent, made for the temple. In these verses, when the author speaks as if Solomon did something, he means that Huram Abi did it, assisted by Solomon’s workers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly throughout this chapter, as the UST does.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Artistic craftsmanship as a form of worship

In this chapter, the author gives a detailed description of many different bronze items that Huram made for the temple. (At the end of the previous chapter he also describes him making the two great pillars.) Beyond having functions that were vital to the priests’ work in the temple area, these were works of art created by a master craftsman. The exquisite detail that Huram worked into these articles, including pomegranates, lilies, and chains, shows the high value that Solomon (Shelomoh) and the Israelites (Israelis) placed on artistic skill in the service of God. The craftsmanship was considered a form of worship, and the beauty of these objects was meant to reflect the glory of God, in whose service they were used.

### The great basin or sea and the bronze stands

The great water basin or sea and the ten bronze stands were central components of the temple’s courtyard. The sea was an enormous bronze basin that held water for the priests to wash themselves, symbolizing ritual purity before entering God’s presence. It rested on twelve bronze oxen, which were not objects of worship but symbolic representations of the twelve tribes of Israel (Yisrael). The bronze stands were elaborate carts used to move smaller basins, also for washing sacrifices. These objects were essential for the sacrificial system, emphasizing that purity was a prerequisite for approaching a holy God. They underscored the meticulous care and religious significance of every detail within the temple complex.

# 2 Chronicles 5 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of Solomon (Shelomoh). It describes how he brought the Box of Yahweh into the temple. It then describes how Yahweh filled the temple with his glory.

1. Conclusion to the construction of the temple (1)
2. Solomon assembles the Israelite (Israeli) leaders to bring the Box into the temple (2–11)
3. As the Israelites (Israelis) worship, Yahweh fills the temple with his glory (12–14)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the Levites’ song in verse 13.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The transfer of the Box of the Covenant to the temple

In this chapter, the author describes how Solomon (Shelomoh) gathered the Israelite leaders for a ceremony to transfer the Box of the Covenant of Yahweh to a permanent home in the temple. The Box was the most sacred object in ancient Israel (Yisrael). It contained the stone tablets that Moses (Mosheh) had put inside it when Yahweh met with the Israelites at Mount Sinai (Sinay) and made his covenant with them. Yahweh was understood to be present in a special way above the Box. Placing the Box in the Holy of Holies inside the temple made it the true center of Israelite worship. The fact that the priests could no longer see the Box once it was placed in the innermost sanctuary emphasized its immense holiness and the sacredness of God’s presence.

# 2 Chronicles 6 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of Solomon (Shelomoh). It describes how he dedicated the temple with an extensive prayer that Yahweh would answer prayers that people offered toward the temple under a variety of difficult circumstances.

1. Solomon tells the Israelites (Israelis) how the temple fulfills Yahweh’s promise (1–11)
2. Solomon dedicates the temple by praying to Yahweh (12–42)
    1. Introduction (12–13)
    2. Prayer for Yahweh to confirm David’s descendants as kings (14–17)
    3. General request for Yahweh to hear prayers addressed to him in the temple (18–21)
    4. Request for Yahweh to do justice when people swear oaths at the temple (22–23)
    5. Request for Yahweh to help the Israelites after enemies defeat them (24–25)
    6. Request for Yahweh to help the Israelites during famine and plague (26–31)
    7. Request for Yahweh to answer the prayers of foreigners (32–33)
    8. Request for Yahweh to help the Israelites when he tells them to fight enemies (34–35)
    9. Request for Yahweh to bring back Israelites who are exiled (36–39)
    10. Conclusion (40–42)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Solomon’s (Shelomoh’s) allusions to Deuteronomy in his prayer of dedication

Most of this chapter consists of Solomon’s prayer of dedication for the temple. In that prayer, he makes many allusions to what Moses (Mosheh) said in the book of Deuteronomy, especially the warnings of what would happen to the Israelites (Israelis) if they were disobedient. In chapters 28 and 30 of Deuteronomy, Moses warned of consequences such as famine, disaster, defeat, and exile if the people turned away from Yahweh. In his prayer, Solomon echoes this language as he prays about such consequences. At the same time, similarly echoing what Moses said, Solomon repeatedly asks that if the Israelites repent, confess their sins, and pray toward the temple, even from exile, Yahweh will hear from heaven, forgive their sins, and restore them. If you have already translated the book of Deuteronomy, try to translate phrases from that book that also appear in Solomon’s prayer the same way you translated them there. This will help readers recognize how Solomon is acknowledging the promises that Yahweh made through Moses and praying that he will fulfill them.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Parallels with 1 Kings and Psalms

Verses 1–39 of this chapter closely parallel 1 Kings 8:1–11. Verses 41–42 closely parallel Psalm 132:8-10. If you have already translated 1 Kings and Psalms, consult your work there, as that will help you translate this chapter.

He does that to ask that this action take place at the same time as the action of someone making a “supplication.” (It is clear that this is the significance of this construction from the way Solomon says “when” or “if” to introduce some other circumstances under which people would pray and under which he is asking Yahweh to respond.) If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning, here and in the rest of the chapter.

Quote: וַ⁠יְהִ֕י עִם־לְבַ֖ב דָּוִ֣יד אָבִ֑⁠י לִ⁠בְנ֣וֹת בַּ֔יִת
Note: Solomon (Shelomoh) is using **it was with the heart of David** as a common expression of his culture to mean “David earnestly wanted” or “David strongly desired.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [And David my father had his heart set on building a temple] or [And David my father earnestly wanted to build a temple]

Quote: וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֶל־דָּוִ֣יד אָבִ֔⁠י יַ֗עַן אֲשֶׁ֤ר הָיָה֙ עִם־לְבָ֣בְ⁠ךָ֔ לִ⁠בְנ֥וֹת בַּ֖יִת לִ⁠שְׁמִ֑⁠י הֱֽטִיב֔וֹתָ כִּ֥י הָיָ֖ה עִם־לְבָבֶֽ⁠ךָ
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh told David my father that because it was with his heart to build a house for his name, he did well that it was with his heart]

Quote: וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֶל־דָּוִ֣יד אָבִ֔⁠י יַ֗עַן אֲשֶׁ֤ר הָיָה֙ עִם־לְבָ֣בְ⁠ךָ֔ לִ⁠בְנ֥וֹת בַּ֖יִת לִ⁠שְׁמִ֑⁠י הֱֽטִיב֔וֹתָ כִּ֥י הָיָ֖ה עִם־לְבָבֶֽ⁠ךָ
Note: It might seem that repeating the expression **it was with your heart** would be to convey extra information in a way that was not natural in your language. If so, you could shorten represent this expression only once in your translation. Alternate translation: [You did well to have it with your heart to build a house for my name]

Quote: רַ֣ק אַתָּ֔ה לֹ֥א תִבְנֶ֖ה הַ⁠בָּ֑יִת כִּ֤י בִנְ⁠ךָ֙ הַ⁠יּוֹצֵ֣א מֵֽ⁠חֲלָצֶ֔י⁠ךָ הֽוּא־יִבְנֶ֥ה הַ⁠בַּ֖יִת לִ⁠שְׁמִֽ⁠י
Note: If you translated the previous verse so that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [However, he, David, would not build the house, but rather his son coming out from his loins, he would be the one to build the house for his name]

Yahweh is stating the pronouns **you** and **he** separately, even though the verbs translated as **you will build** and **he will build** already includes their meanings. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast. Alternate translation: [you will not be the one who will build … he will be the one who will build]

The implication of the expression **coming out from your loins** is that David would be the actual father of this son (that is, this would not be an adopted or foster son). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. 2sa/07/12.md). Alternate translation: [your own biological son]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is speaking as if Yahweh’s **word**, or what Yahweh said, were an object that Yahweh could **raise up**. He means that Yahweh will cause what he said to happen. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [so that Yahweh may make what he said happen] Alternate translation: [And Yahweh has made happen the things that he spoke about]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is speaking as if he had actually **arisen** or stood up instead of David. He means that he has taken his late father’s former role as king. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I have taken the place of David my father] or [And I have succeeded David my father]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is speaking as if he had actually **arisen**, that is, as if he had risen into the air or up to an elevated location. In contexts such as this, this expression describes a person becoming powerful or obtaining a powerful position. Alternate translation: [And I have come to power]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is using sitting on the **throne of Israel (Yisrael)** to represent being the king of the Israelites (Israelis) and having the authority to rule them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I am ruling the Israelites]

It might seem that the expression **where the Covenant of Yahweh is there** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [where the Covenant of Yahweh is] or [that contains the Covenant of Yahweh]

Here, the **Covenant of Yahweh** represents the two stone tablets that the author describes in [5:10](../05/10.md), on which the terms of the covenant between Yahweh and the Israelites (Israelis) were written. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [where the two stone tablets are] or [that contains the two stone tablets]
See how you translated the same expression in [5:10](../05/10.md). Alternate translation: [he made]
See how you translated the same expression in [5:10](../05/10.md). Alternate translation: [the Israelites (Israelis)]

In this context, this expression indicates that Solomon (Shelomoh) turned around again and faced the altar of burnt offerings that was in the temple court. (While he was **in front of** the crowd of Israelites (Israelis) from their perspective, from his perspective, they were behind him.) Alternate translation: [facing]

Solomon (Shelomoh) spreading out **his palms** was a symbolic action by which he showed he was praying to Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And he spread out his palms in prayer]

The author is using the term **now** to introduce background information that will help readers understand what is happening in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Quote: חָמֵ֨שׁ אַמּ֜וֹת אָרְכּ֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠חָמֵ֤שׁ אַמּוֹת֙ רָחְבּ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠אַמּ֥וֹת שָׁל֖וֹשׁ קוֹמָת֑⁠וֹ
Note: See how you represented the length of cubits in chapter 3, and represent them the same way here.

Solomon (Shelomoh) kneeling on **his knees** was a further symbolic action by which he showed he was praying to Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he knelt reverently on his knees … and he spread out his palms toward the heavens in prayer]
It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [and he knelt down]

The words **you** and **your** are singular here and through verse 42 because they refer to Yahweh. (It is also singular in the expression “your sons” in [6:16](../06/16.md) since it refers to David.) So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Solomon (Shelomoh) is speaking to Yahweh of himself and the Israelites (Israelis) in the third person as **your servants** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [with us, your servants]
See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Chronicles of how the author and characters use the idea of walking to mean living. Alternate translation: [who live as they should in your presence]

Here, the **heart** represents people’s motives and desires. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [wholeheartedly] or [in complete devotion]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [just as you spoke to him]

See how you translated the similar expression in [6:4](../06/04.md). Alternate translation: [And you have fulfilled by your hand what you spoke by your mouth] or [And you have fulfilled by your own action what you spoke by your mouth]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is using **as this day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “as is true right now” or “as can be seen at this present time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as is the case right now]
See how you translated the similar expression in [2:7](../02/07.md).

Quote: לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר לֹא־יִכָּרֵ֨ת לְ⁠ךָ֥ אִישׁ֙ מִ⁠לְּ⁠פָנַ֔⁠י יוֹשֵׁ֖ב עַל־כִּסֵּ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל רַ֠ק אִם־יִשְׁמְר֨וּ בָנֶ֜י⁠ךָ אֶת־דַּרְכָּ֗⁠ם לָ⁠לֶ֨כֶת֙ בְּ⁠ת֣וֹרָתִ֔⁠י כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָלַ֖כְתָּ לְ⁠פָנָֽ⁠י
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [when you told him that a man to him would not be cut off from to your face, sitting on the throne of Israel (Yisrael), if only his sons would keep their way, to walk in your law just as he had walked to your face]

Quote: לֹא־יִכָּרֵ֨ת לְ⁠ךָ֥ אִישׁ֙ מִ⁠לְּ⁠פָנַ֔⁠י יוֹשֵׁ֖ב עַל־כִּסֵּ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
Note: This is a double negative, consisting of the negative **not** and the verb **cut off**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [a man to you will always be sitting on the throne of Israel (Yisrael) to my face]

The expression **will not be cut off** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will not cut off a man to you]

Here Yahweh is speaking as David’s descendants could be **cut off** from the throne. This image depicts someone being removed from power as if they were being physically separated from the throne, like a branch being cut from a tree. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a man to you will not be removed] or [I will not remove a man to you]

The phrase **a man to you** is a possessive form. It means “a man who belongs to you,” and it describes someone who is a male descendant of David. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [one of your male descendants]

Quote: יִשְׁמְר֨וּ בָנֶ֜י⁠ךָ אֶת־דַּרְכָּ֗⁠ם לָ⁠לֶ֨כֶת֙ בְּ⁠ת֣וֹרָתִ֔⁠י כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָלַ֖כְתָּ לְ⁠פָנָֽ⁠י
Note: See how you translated the similar expression in [6:14](../06/14.md). Alternate translation: [your descendants will live as they should by obeying my law, just as you have lived in my presence]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is using the term **word** to represent what God said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may what you said when you spoke to your servant David, my father, be confirmed]

The expression **may … be confirmed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [may you confirm your word that you spoke] or [may you confirm what you said when you spoke]

Quote: כִּ֚י הַֽ⁠אֻמְנָ֔ם יֵשֵׁ֧ב אֱלֹהִ֛ים אֶת־הָ⁠אָדָ֖ם עַל־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ
Note: Solomon (Shelomoh) is using the question form to make a strong statement. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [But God will not truly dwell with man on the earth!]

Even though Solomon (Shelomoh) is addressing God directly, he is speaking of him in the third person to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [you, God]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [people] or [human beings]
See how you translated the same expression in [2:4](../02/04.md). Alternate translation: [Indeed]

In this context, the term **heavens** refers to the sky, while the phrase **the heavens of the heavens** describes the spiritual realm beyond the sky that is God’s abode. Translators whose languages have separate words for the sky and for God’s abode may be able to use those terms here in their translations. Alternate translation: [the sky and heaven itself]

Here, Solomon (Shelomoh) is speaking as if paying attention were actually to **turn** toward someone. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yet may you pay attention]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [to my prayer and to my supplication … I am praying]

Together, the terms **prayer** and **supplication** express a single idea. The word **supplication** tells what kind of **prayer** this is. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [to my prayer for help] or [to the requests I am making as I pray]

See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Chronicles of this use of the term “listen.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate explicitly in your translation, here and in verses 20 and 21, that the term in the context of Solomon’s (Shelomoh’s) prayer means “answer.” Alternate translation: [to answer the cry and the prayer]

In this context, the terms **cry** and **prayer** mean similar things. Solomon (Shelomoh) is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to listen to the fervent prayer] or [to answer the fervent prayer]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [the prayer that your servant is offering]

Here, **to your face** represents being in the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your presence]

The expression **may be opened** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that you may open your eyes to this temple] or [that you may keep your eyes open to this temple]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is using Yahweh’s **eyes** to represent his sight. He means that he wants Yahweh to be watching the temple so that he is aware of people who are praying to him there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that you may watch this temple and be aware of people who are praying to you here]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is referring to all of time by naming its two major components, **day** and **night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the time]

Here, Yahweh’s **name** represents his presence and authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [people would worship you there] or [your reputation would be known there]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is not referring to a specific **prayer**. He means prayers in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the prayers] or [any prayer]

Here and in verses 21 and 26, Solomon (Shelomoh) refers to people directing their prayers toward the temple. Praying in the direction of the temple was a symbolic action by which worshipers showed that they recognized the temple as the place where Yahweh was especially present. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [will direct to you at this temple] or [will pray to you while facing this temple where you are especially present]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is not referring to a specific **supplication**. He means supplications in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any supplication … that they may make]

See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of Solomon’s (Shelomoh’s) use of the explicit pronoun “you” in this phrase that he repeats several times in his prayer. Alternate translation: [And as they are praying, may you hear]

In the context of this prayer, the term “hear” has the same sense as the term “listen.” It means to answer a prayer by doing what a person has requested. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this explicitly in your translation, here and in the many similar instances in the rest of this prayer. Alternate translation: [may you answer from the place of your dwelling]

The terms **from the place of your dwelling** and **from the heavens** mean similar things. Solomon (Shelomoh) is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase, here and in similar instances in the rest of this prayer. Alternate translation: [in the heavens where you dwell]

The phrase **hear and forgive** expresses a single idea. The word **forgive** tells in what way Solomon (Shelomoh) is asking Yahweh to **hear** (that is, answer) the prayers that various people will pray when they are suffering because they have sinned. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way, here and in similar contexts in the rest of this prayer. Alternate translation: [and may you answer by forgiving]

In this verse, Solomon (Shelomoh) is introducing the first part of a possible condition. He is asking Yahweh to do the things he describes in the next verse if this condition happens. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If someone sins, a man against his neighbor] or [Suppose someone sins, a man against his neighbor]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is using ** a man against his neighbor** as a common expression of his culture to describe what one person might do to another person. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Suppose one person sins against another]

The implication is that it is uncertain whether a person has actually wronged another person, and so resolution through an oath at the altar is required. You could indicate this uncertainty in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Suppose one person may have sinned against another]

The pronoun **he** refers to the offended party, while the pronoun **him** refers to the person who may have committed the offense. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the neighbor lifts an oath against the man to adjure the man]

The author is using **lifts an oath** as a common expression of his culture to mean “makes someone swear an oath.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he puts him under an oath] or [and he makes him swear an oath]

The implication is that the person who may have committed the offense would have to swear an oath at the altar that he was innocent. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [that he is innocent]

Here, the term **oath** represents the person who is making the oath. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and a person who is under such an oath comes] or [and a person who is required to swear such an oath comes]

Here, **to the face of your altar** represents being in front of the altar. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of your altar]

By **in this house**, Solomon (Shelomoh) specifically means in the courtyard of the temple, where the altar was located. (Only priests could enter the temple building.) You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the courtyard of this temple]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is first describing one event, in which Yahweh would **act** to punish the **wicked** and reward the **righteous** (as the rest of the verse describes). He is then describing another event that would precede it, in which Yahweh would **judge** people as either righteous or wicked. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they would happen. Alternate translation: [and judge your servants and act]

The phrase **act and judge** expresses a single idea. The word **act** tells in what way Yahweh would **judge**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [and actively judge]

The author is using the adjectives **wicked** and **righteous** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [the wicked person … the righteous person] or [the person who is wicked … the person who is righteous]

Solomon (Shelomoh) is using **to put his way on his head** as a common expression of his culture to ask Yahweh to hold the **wicked** person morally and legally responsible and punish him for his **way**, that is, what he has done. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to bring down on his own head what he has done] or [to punish him for the wrong thing he has done]

Quote: וְֽ⁠אִם־יִנָּגֵ֞ף עַמְּ⁠ךָ֧ יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י אוֹיֵ֖ב כִּ֣י יֶֽחֶטְאוּ־לָ֑⁠ךְ
Note: See how you translated the similar expression in [6:22](../06/22.md). Alternate translation: [Suppose your people Israel (Yisrael) are struck to the face of an enemy because they have sinned against you]

Quote: וְֽ⁠אִם־יִנָּגֵ֞ף עַמְּ⁠ךָ֧ יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י אוֹיֵ֖ב כִּ֣י יֶֽחֶטְאוּ־לָ֑⁠ךְ
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Suppose your people Israel (Yisrael) sin against you and, as a result, they are struck to the face of an enemy]
See the discussion of the term “struck” in the introduction to 2 Chronicles. Alternate translation: [Suppose your people Israel (Yisrael) are defeated to the face of an enemy]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of an **enemy**, that is, opposing an enemy in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Suppose your people Israel (Yisrael) are defeated in front of an enemy] or [Suppose your people Israel are defeated as they fight against an enemy]

The expression **are struck** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Suppose an enemy defeats your people Israel (Yisrael) as they fight against them]

Here, Solomon (Shelomoh) is speaking as if the Israelites (Israelis), within the possible condition he is describing, **turn back** to walk toward Yahweh again after walking away from him. He means that they would stop sinning and start living again in the manner in which God wants people to live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they repent] or [and they stop sinning]

Here, Yahweh’s **name** represents his reputation, and in this context, specifically his deserved reputation as a righteous God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and they acknowledge your righteous character] or [and they acknowledge that you were right to have punished them in this way]

Together, the words **pray** and **supplicate** expresses a single idea. The word **supplicate** tells what the people would be doing as they **pray**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [and they pray for help]
See how you translated the similar expression in [6:20](../06/20.md). Alternate translation: [toward this temple as a place where you are present]

The pronoun **them** refers to any Israelites (Israelis) an enemy may have captured and taken prisoner. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and bring back any prisoners whom the enemy has captured]

Solomon (Shelomoh) means that Yahweh **gave** the **land** to the present and future generations of Israelites (Israelis) as something they would inherit from their **fathers** or ancestors, to whom he originally gave it. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to their ancestors and that they have inherited]

Quote: בְּ⁠הֵעָצֵ֧ר הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֛יִם וְ⁠לֹֽא־יִהְיֶ֥ה מָטָ֖ר כִּ֣י יֶֽחֶטְאוּ־לָ֑⁠ךְ

# 2 Chronicles 7 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of Solomon (Shelomoh). It describes what happened after Solomon had finished dedicating the temple with his prayer.

1. Fire comes down from heaven and Yahweh’s glory fills the temple (1–3)
2. Solomon and the people offer sacrifices (4–7)
3. Solomon and the people celebrate the Feast of Shelters (8–10)
4. Yahweh appears to Solomon in a dream for a second time, promising blessings for obedience but warning of punishment for disobedience. (11–22)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the songs in verses 3 and 6.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Blessings for obedience, punishments for disobedience

After the dedication of the temple, Yahweh appeared to Solomon (Shelomoh) a second time. He repeated the covenant promises he had made to David. Yahweh promised to establish Solomon’s throne forever if he and his descendants remained faithful and obedient to him. However, he also warned of severe consequences if they became devoted to other gods instead and worshiped them. This divine warning highlights a central theme of the Old Testament: there would be blessings for obedience, but there would be severe punishment for disobedience, especially for disobedience in the form of living in the way that followers of foreign gods lived. The nation’s well-being was directly linked to the fidelity of the king and people to Yahweh. This covenantal relationship provides the background to the events that unfold later in the rest of this story.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “serve other gods and bow down to them”

In verse 19, Yahweh warns Solomon that his descendants who become kings must not “serve other gods” and “prostrate themselves to them.” When applied to “other gods,” the term “serve” refers to honoring them by living as their followers did, building shrines for them, and generally following religious practices. To prostrate oneself to these gods (physically bowing to idols that represented them in a shrine or temple) was a symbolic action of surrender to them as one’s lord. It represented a definitive further step, beyond the idea of “serving” or honoring them. This would provoke Yahweh’s severe judgment, as he describes in verses 20–22. Later in the book, we hear how King Manasseh (Menasheh) took this further definitive step. The author reports in 33:3 that “he set up altars for the Baals, and he made Asherahs, and he prostrated himself to all of the army of the heavens.” Because the difference between “serving” and bowing down or prostrating oneself has this significance, we recommend that you do not combine these two terms, even if you sometimes combine similar terms in your translation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain in the text of your translation or in a footnote the significance of bowing down as ultimately commit oneself to another god.

# 2 Chronicles 9 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the author’s account of the reign of Solomon (Shelomoh). It describes further events in Solomon’s reign.

1. The Queen of Sheba (Sheva) visits Solomon (1–12)
2. Solomon’s great wealth and wisdom (13–28)
3. Conclusion to the reign of Solomon (29–31)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The Queen of Sheba

The Queen of Sheba’s visit to King Solomon highlights his wealth and wisdom. Having learned of Solomon’s reputation, the Queen undertakes a long journey (probably from modern-day Yemen) to see whether he can answer some difficult questions that trouble her. Her visit shows how far his reputation, and with it the reputation of Yahweh, had spread. The Queen is so impressed by Solomon’s wisdom and wealth and by the splendor of his kingdom that she praises Yahweh. Her acknowledgment of Yahweh’s favor to Solomon and Israel (Yisrael) brings glory to him and confirms the blessings that he promised to the Davidic line. This story underscores the global recognition of God’s blessing on Israel through Solomon’s reign, and it serves as a significant indication of his kingdom’s influence.

### Sources of Solomon’s (Shelomoh’s) wealth

Solomon’s kingdom was strategically located at the crossroads of major trade routes, including those running through the Arabian (Aravi) Peninsula and up from Egypt (Mitsrayim). This gave him control over the movement of goods, including gold, spices, and other valuable commodities. He could therefore charge taxes, tolls, and duties. The author describes in [9:14](../09/14.md) how Solomon derived such income from “men of the searchers,” that is, men who traveled to distant lands to find goods for trade, and from “traders,” that is, local merchants who bought goods from traveling merchants and sold them within the country. He also describes how Solomon received income from the “kings of the Arab.” That phrase seems to refer to rulers of independent or semi-independent Arabian kingdoms located to the south and east of Israel. These kings apparently made gifts to Solomon from time to time in exchange for peaceful trade relations and as a sign of submission to his superior military and economic power. The 666 talents of gold that the author mentions in the previous verse might have been a fixed, yearly tax or tribute from Solomon’s main vassal states, while the gold from the Arabian kings came as gifts or offerings for trade access. The gifts from the Queen of Sheba (Sheva), for example, would have been a significant, yet one-time, contribution to Solomon’s wealth, separate from his yearly tribute.

# 2 Chronicles 10 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the author’s account of the reign of Rehoboam (Rehav’am), Solomon’s (Shelomoh’s) son. It tells how Rehoboam unwisely refused to allow the Israelites (Israelis) to work less hard for him than they had for his father. As a result, the kingdom that David and Solomon had ruled split into two kingdoms, Israel (Yisrael) in the north and Judah (Yehudah) in the south.

1. The Israelites assemble and ask Rehoboam for leniency (1–5)
2. Rehoboam consults his father’s advisers and his young friends (6–11)
3. Rehoboam follows the advice of his young friends and the Israelites revolt (12–19)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Israel splits

In spite of his fabulous wealth, Solomon had over-taxed his own people and forced them to work too hard. When the people requested that his son Rehoboam, who succeeded him as king, reduce taxes and forced labor, he replied that he would be even harsher than his father. This caused the ten northern tribes to revolt and appoint Jeroboam (Yarov’am) as their king. These northern tribes became the kingdom of Israel. Only the united tribe of Judah and Benjamin (Benyamin) remained loyal to Rehoboam. They became the kingdom of Judah.

### Why did Rehoboam (Rehav’am) send Hadoram out?

The author describes in 12:18 how, after the Israelites (Israelis) rejected Rehoboam as their king, he sent Hadoram, his officer in charge of forced labor, to speak with them. The Israelites responded by stoning Hadoram to death. Rehoboam then had to flee to Jerusalem (Yerushalem) in his chariot to save his own life. It may seem that Rehoboam should have anticipated this outcome and not sent Hadoram to speak with the people. This shows that he truly did have bad judgment because he was relying on his younger, inexperienced friends instead of the older men who had attended his father Solomon (Shelomoh) and heard his wisdom. Sending Hadoram to the people signaled Rehoboam’s intent to continue and enforce the harsh labor policies established under his father Solomon, which the people deeply resented. Rather than seeking dialogue or reconciliation, Rehoboam acted out of arrogance or misjudgment, believing wrongly that a show of authority through his officer would quell resistance.

# 2 Chronicles 11 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of Rehoboam (Rehav’am). It describes how he made his kingdom of Judah (Yehudah) militarily strong and how priests, Levites, and other Israelites (Israelis) who wanted to worship Yahweh moved to his kingdom. It also describes his wives and children.

1. Yahweh forbids Rehoboam to attack the northern kingdom of Israel (Yisrael) (1–4)
2. Rehoboam fortifies his southern kingdom of Judah (5–12)
3. Faithful priests, Levites, and other Israelites move to Judah (13–17)
4. Rehoboam’s wives and children (18–23)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Parallel with 1 Kings

Verses 1–4 of this chapter closely parallel 1 Kings 12:22-24. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, consult your work there, as that will help you translate this chapter.

# 2 Chronicles 12 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the author’s account of the reign of Rehoboam (Rehav’am). It tells how he became unfaithful to Yahweh and how Yahweh punished him by allowing Shishak, the king of Egypt (Mitsrayim), to conquer Jerusalem (Yerushalem) and plunder it.

1. Rehoboam is unfaithful to Yahweh and Shishak invades Judah (Yehudah) (1–4)
2. The prophet Shemaiah (Shemayah) explains that Yahweh is punishing Rehoboam (5–8)
3. Shishak plunders Jerusalem but Yahweh prevents its destruction (9–12)
4. Conclusion to the reign of Rehoboam (13–16)

In this context, the author is using the term **Israel (Yisrael)** to identify these people as Israelites (Israelis), not as subjects of the northern kingdom of Israel rather than the southern kingdom of Judah (Yehudah). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers, here and in verse 6. Alternate translation: [and all of Judah forsook the law of Yahweh with him] or [and all of the people of his kingdom forsook the law of Yahweh with him]

# 2 Chronicles 13 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the author’s account of the reign of Abijah (Aviyah), Rehoboam’s (Rehav’am’s) son. It tells mostly about how he fought against King Jeroboam (Yarov’am) of Israel (Yisrael).

1. Introduction to Abijah’s reign and his war with Jeroboam (1–3)
2. Abijah warns Jeroboam and his soldiers about their unfaithfulness to Yahweh (4–12)
3. Yahweh enables the Judeans (Yehudim) to defeat the Israelites (Israelis) (13–20)
4. Conclusion to the reign of Abijah (21–22)

# 2 Chronicles 14 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the author’s account of the reign of Asa, Abijah’s (Aviyah’s) son. It describes how he restored the worship of Yahweh in Judah (Yehudah) and how he fortified that kingdom. It also tells how a very large army attacked Judah but Yahweh enables the Judeans (Yehudim) to defeat it.

1. Introduction to Asa’s reign and his restoration of the worship of Yahweh (1–5)
2. How Asa fortified the kingdom of Judah (6–8)
3. The Cushites (Kushim) attack Judah but Yahweh enables the Judeans to defeat them (9–15)

# 2 Chronicles 15 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of Asa. It describes how, with the encouragement of the prophet Azariah (Azaryah), he led the Judeans (Yehudim) to renew their covenant with Yahweh.

1. Azariah encourages Asa and the Judeans to be faithful to Yahweh (1–7)
2. Asa destroys idols and repairs Yahweh’s altar (8)
3. Asa assembles the Judeans for a covenant renewal ceremony (9–15)
4. Asa deposes the idolatrous queen mother and dedicates gifts to Yahweh (16–19)

The author is using **the Spirit of God was upon him** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the Spirit of God inspired Azariah (Azaryah) to speak. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the Spirit of God inspired him]

# 2 Chronicles 16 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the author’s account of the reign of Asa. It describes how he depended on an alliance with the king of Aram instead of on Yahweh when King Baasha (Baesha) of Israel (Yisrael) started building a fortress city on their border. It also describes how the prophet Hanani corrected him for this but Asa put Hanani in prison instead of accepting the correction. The chapter concludes by relating how Asa died of a serious disease.

1. King Baasha of Israel threatens Judah (Yehudah) and Asa relies on an alliance with Aram (1–6)
2. The prophet Hanani tells Asa he should have relied on Yahweh instead (7–10)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Was Asa not really wholeheartedly devoted to Yahweh?

The author says in 15:17 that “the heart of Asa was whole all of his days,” meaning that he was wholeheartedly devoted to Yahweh for his entire life. However, when the prophet Hanani corrects Asa in this chapter for depending on a foreign alliance, he tells him that Yahweh strongly helps “those whose heart is whole toward him” and that he therefore has “acted foolishly regarding this.” This is not actually a contradiction. The author means in 15:17 that Asa did not worship any false god during his lifetime. He worshiped only Yahweh. Hanani is speaking to a different issue. He is telling him that if he had depended entirely on Yahweh for help, Yahweh would have helped him powerfully. Unfortunately Asa did not do that, either in his conflict with Baasha or later in his sickness, when, according to 16:12, he sought help only from doctors, not from Yahweh. So in the previous chapter, Asa’s heart being whole toward Yahweh refers to exclusive worship. In this chapter, Asa’s heart not being whole toward Yahweh refers to his failure to depend on him rather than on people for help.

### Why did Asa oppress some of his subjects?

The author reports in 16:10 that when Asa put the prophet Hanani in prison, he “oppressed some of the people at that time.” The author says nothing more specific about who these people were or why Asa oppressed them. However, the context suggests that these were people who supported Hanani and who similarly told Asa that he should not have made an alliance with the king of Aram. Instead, he should have trusted Yahweh to help him. It appears that Yahweh judged and punished Asa for imprisoning Hanani and for oppressing these people. Asa put Hanani in prison in the stocks, that is, with restraints on his feet, and Asa got a serious and ultimately fatal disease in his own feet. While the author does not draw a specific connection between the unjust and cruel punishment and the disease, biblical writers expected their readers to recognize the appropriateness of such divine judgments, by which people, especially if they resisted correction, got what they deserved for what they had done.

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the author’s account of the reign of Jehoshaphat (Yehoshafat), Asa’s son. It describes how he was loyal to Yahweh and continued to strengthen the kingdom of Judah (Yehudah). It also tells how he sent priests and Levites among the Judeans (Yehudim) to teach them Yahweh’s law.

# 2 Chronicles 18 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of Jehoshaphat (Yehoshafat). It describes how, once he had become rich and powerful, he made an alliance with King Ahab (Ahav) of Israel (Yisrael). Ahab persuaded him to lead his soldiers to attack the city of Ramoth (Ramot) Gilead with his own army. The prophet Micaiah (Mikayah) warned that the attack would fail and Ahab would be killed, and that is what happened.

1. Ahab persuades Jehoshaphat to attack Ramoth Gilead with him (1–3)
2. Jehoshaphat asks Ahab to seek Yahweh’s guidance (4–11)
3. Micaiah brings a message from Yahweh saying Ahab will be killed (12–27)
4. Ahab and Jehoshaphat attack Ramoth Gilead, and Ahab is killed (28–34)

# 2 Chronicles 19 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of Jehoshaphat (Yehoshafat). It describes how the prophet Jehu (Yehu) rebuked him for making an alliance with the wicked king Ahab (Ahav). In response, Jehoshaphat personally went throughout Judah (Yehudah) to encourage the people to be loyal to Yahweh. He appointed judges to settle disputes and resolve issues honestly according to Yahweh’s law.

1. Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat (1–3)
2. Jehoshaphat encourages the Judeans (Yehudim) to be loyal to Yahweh (4)
3. Jehoshaphat appoints judges (5–11)

# 2 Chronicles 20 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the author’s account of the reign of Jehoshaphat (Yehoshafat). It describes how a huge army of Moabites (Moavim), Ammonites (Amonim), and Edomites (Edomim) attacked the kingdom of Judah (Yehudah). Jehoshaphat and the people gathered and prayed to Yahweh for help. Through a prophet, Yahweh promised that he would defeat them and the Judeans (Yehudim) would not have to fight at all. Yahweh made these enemies fight and kill each other, and all the Judeans had to do was gather the plunder.

1. A huge army attacks Judah and the Judeans assemble to ask Yahweh for help (1–4)
2. Jehoshaphat leads the people in prayer (5–12)
3. Jahaziel (Yahaziel) prophesies that Yahweh will defeat these enemies (13–19)
4. The Judeans put the Levite singers at the front of their army (20–21)
5. Yahweh makes the enemy soldiers fight and kill each other (22–24)
6. The Judeans gather the plunder and celebrate (25–30)
7. Conclusion to the reign of Jehoshaphat (31–37)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with Jehoshaphat’s exhortation in verse 20 and the Levites’ song in verse 21.

The standard written Hebrew text as we have it today reads “Ammonites (Amonim).” This reading, however, does not seem to make sense, since the author has already mentioned **the sons of Ammon (Amon)**, so the Ammonites would not be an additional group. Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have reversed two consonants of the original text, resulting in this word. With those consonants in the other order, it would say “Maunites,” which seems to fit better the meaning of this passage. The Maunites lived on Mount Seir (Se’ir) in Edom, and in verse 22 the author describes the invading army as “the sons of Ammon, Moab (Moav), and Mount Seir.” Here he may be using one group from Edom to represent the Edomites (Edomim) generally. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [from the Maunites] or [from the Edomites]

Most ancient manuscripts read “Aram.” The ULT follows that reading. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense, since an army coming from **Aram** would not be coming **from beyond the sea**. One ancient manuscript and one ancient version read “from Edom,” which is the direction from which soldiers of these people groups would be coming. The reference in verse 10 to “Mount Seir (Se’ir)” in Edom seems to support this reading. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. # 2 Chronicles 21 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the author’s account of the reign of Jehoram (Yehoram), Jehoshaphat’s (Yehoshafat’s) son. It describes how he was an evil king because his wife Athaliah (Atalyah) was a daughter of Ahab (Ahav). This chapter relates how he killed all of his brothers and how he failed to reconquer the Edomites (Edomim) when they rebelled. It tells how the prophet Elijah (Eliyah) sent him a message from Yahweh, rebuking him and prophesying that enemies would take away his family and possessions and that Jehoram himself would die of a lingering, painful disease. That is just what happened.

1. Introduction to the reign of Jehoram (1–7)
2. Jehoram fails to reconquer the Edomites (8–11)
3. Elijah rebukes Jehoram and prophesies his ruin and death (12–15)
4. The Philistines (Pelishtim) and Arabians (Aravim) take away Jehoram’s family and possessions (16–17)
4. Jehoram dies of a lingering, painful disease (18–20)
