# 2 Chronicles 22 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the author’s account of the reign of Ahaziah (Ahazyah), Jehoram’s (Yehoram’s) son. It describes how he too was an evil king, since his mother Athaliah (Atalyah) was a daughter of Ahab (Ahav). This chapter relates how he allied himself with Jehoram, the son of Ahab, and was therefore killed with Jehoram when Jehu (Yehu), the son of Nimshi, carried out Yahweh’s judgment against Ahab’s family. This chapter then tells how Athaliah tried to kill all of Ahaziah’s sons (her own grandsons) so that she could rule Judah (Yehudah) and how Ahaziah’s half-sister Jehoshabeath (Yehoshav’at) was able to save his infant son Joash (Yoash).

1. Introduction to the reign of Ahaziah (1–4)
2. Ahaziah joins Jehoram in attacking Ramoth (Ramot) Gilead, where Jehoram is wounded (5–6)
3. Jehu kills Ahaziah when he comes to visit Jehoram in his recovery (7–9)
4. Athaliah tries to kill all of Ahaziah’s sons but Jehoshabeath rescues Joash (10–12)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The meaning of “camp” in 22:1

In 22:1, the author refers to “the band having come with the Arabians (Aravim) into the camp.” He is speaking as if the center of Jerusalem (Yerushalem), the location of the royal palace and Yahweh’s temple, had actually been a “camp.” He uses the same image in [31:2](../31/02.md) when he calls the temple the “camp of Yahweh.” If you have already translated the book of 1 Chronicles, you will have seen in several places (1 Chronicles 6:32, 6:48, 9:18, and 9:19) how the author uses elements from earlier in the Israelites’ (Israelis’s) history to represent later ones in order to depict the continuity of their community down through the generations. Here he is recalling how the Israelites moved through the wilderness as a camp as Yahweh protected them and led them on their way from Egypt (Mitsrayim) to Canaan (Kena’an). He is doing that to stress how Jehoram (Yehoram) was unfaithful to the covenant with Yahweh and thereby put the very existence of the community at risk. He describes in 21:17 how the invaders plundered the royal palace, and here he is using the palace-temple complex at the core of Jerusalem, which they breached, to represent the whole community that the Davidic kings ruled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly in your translation. A note to 22:1 suggests one way to do that, and the UST models another way to do that.

# 2 Chronicles 23 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the author’s account of how the high priest Jehoiada (Yehoyada) had the Judeans (Yehudim) anoint Joash (Yoash), the surviving son of Ahaziah (Ahazyah), as their next king. It describes how he protected Joash from Athaliah (Atalyah) and her followers and how he had her executed to restore peace and legitimate government to Judah (Yehudah).

1. Jehoiada recruits military and civic leaders to support and protect Joash (1–7)
2. Jehoiada and the leaders anoint Joash as the new king (8–11)
3. Athaliah protests but is executed (12–15)
4. The Judeans restore the worship of Yahweh and enthrone Joash (16–21)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Exceptional permission to enter holy places

As Jehoiada (Yehoyada) briefs the military and civic leaders on his plans to establish Joash (Yoash) as the new king, he tells them “all of the people shall be in the courtyards of the house of Yahweh” (23:5) and that no one should enter “the house of Yahweh except the priests and the ministering ones of the Levites” (23:6). He seems to be indicating that some people will be allowed in places where they ordinarily could not go. By “the courtyards,” he seems to mean both the outer courtyard, where all Israelites (Israelis) could go, and the inner courtyard, where only priests and Levites could go. By “the house of Yahweh,” he seems to mean the temple building, into which only priests, not Levites, could go. Some interpreters have suggested understanding “the courtyards” to be an emphatic plural referring to the size and various areas of the outer courtyard and “the house of Yahweh” to mean the most sacred parts of temple complex, the building and the inner courtyard. However, the author describes later in the book how King Hezekiah (Hizkiyah) interceded with Yahweh for Israelites who ate the Passover without purifying themselves as the law required. Hezekiah asked Yahweh to treat people favorably “everyone who has prepared his heart,” and Yahweh did. So it would be consistent with the author’s message for him to be describing exceptional arrangements under crucial circumstances here in chapter 23. Jehoiada goes on to say in 23:6 that “all of the people shall keep the keeping of Yahweh.” He seems to mean that after this, in all other circumstances, the people, priests, and Levites are to obey the instructions in the law about who may go where. But the restoration of the worship of Yahweh in Judah (Yehudah) requires these extraordinary arrangements, which the people may follow without guilt because of their loyal intentions. This illustrates the author’s overall message, that while the identity of the nation and the continuity of its worship depend on carefully following the instructions in the law, what ultimately matters is a heartfelt desire to honor Yahweh.

### Was there a temple to Baal (Ba’al) in Jerusalem (Yerushalem) near the temple?

The author says in 24:17 that after installing Joash as the new king, “all of the people entered the house of Baal, and they tore it down.” This suggests that there was a temple to Baal in Jerusalem near the temple. It is possible that Jehoram (Yehoram) built this temple, since the book records that he worshiped the same idols that the kings descended from Ahab (Ahav) worshiped (21:13). The author does not specifically that he did, but if it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this in the text of your translation or in a footnote. You might say, for example, that the people “entered the temple to Baal that Jehoram had built near Yahweh’s temple, and they tore it down.”

# 2 Chronicles 24 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the author’s account of the reign of Joash (Yoash), Ahaziah’s (Ahazyah’s) son. It describes how he was at first a good king because of the influence of the high priest Jehoiada (Yehoyada). It relates how he collected money to repair Yahweh’s temple. But the chapter then describes how, after Jehoiada died, the leaders of Judah (Yehudah) persuaded Joash to worship idols instead of Yahweh. It tells how Joash persisted in idolatry even though many prophets warned him. Joash even arranged the murder of Zechariah (Zekaryah), the son of Jehoiada, who was warning him. The chapter finally describes how a small Aramean army defeated the Judeans (Yehudim) and wounded Joash so badly that two of his officials were able to murder him on his sickbed.

1. Introduction to the reign of Joash (1–3)
2. Joash collects money and repairs Yahweh’s temple (4–14)
3. After Jehoiada dies, Joash becomes an idolater and has Zechariah killed (15–22)
4. The Arameans wound Joash and his officials murder him (23–26)
5. Conclusion to the reign of Joash (27)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Were vessels made for the temple from the tribute money or not?

The author says in 24:14 that the men overseeing the repair work in the temple “brought the remainder of the silver” to “the king and Jehoiada (Yehoyada)” and “they made vessels for the house of Yahweh.” However, the parallel account in 2 Kings 12:13 says that articles for the temple “were not made from the silver brought to the house of Yahweh.” This seems at first to be a contradiction, but it is not. The author of 2 Kings says that they did not make articles from the silver “because they gave it to doers of the work” (12:14). The author of Chronicles says specifically that “when they finished, they brought the remainder of the silver” (24:14). So the explanation is that they did not make articles from the silver while the work progressed, but they did do that once it was finished.

### Why did the Judean (Yehudi) princes ask to abandon Yahweh and worship false gods, and why did Joash (Yoash) agree?

Readers of 2 Chronicles are often surprised when they hear that Joash, who eagerly wanted to repair Yahweh’s temple when he was younger (24:4), later became an idolater and persecuted and even killed Yahweh’s prophets. The explanation seems to be that after the death of the high priest Jehoiada, who had protected him, raised him, and advised him, Joash came under the influence of “the princes of Judah (Yehudah),” that is, the leaders of the clans of that tribe. It appears that, away from the influence of the temple and the kings, people in many parts of Judah continued to follow pagan practices. As the author says in 21:33, “the people still did not establish their heart to the God of their fathers” even after the reigns of the godly kings Asa and Jehoshaphat (Yehoshafat). The author records in 24:17 that these princes came and bowed down to Joash. That was the gesture in this culture for making a request, but it seems that it was also flattering for the young king to have these clan leaders bow down to him and that this made him eager to please them. To indicate that a change in influence was likely responsible, you may wish to begin verse 17 with a contrasting word such as “But.”

# 2 Chronicles 25 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the author’s account of the reign of Amaziah (Amatsyah), Joash’s (Yoash’s) son. It describes how he was a good king at first, following the law of Moses (Mosheh) and relying on Yahweh rather than on mercenary troops. But the chapter then relates how, after he defeated the Edomites (Edomim) and brought their gods back to Judah (Yehudah) as war trophies, he started worshiping those gods. He refused to listen to a prophet who tried to warn him about doing that. The chapter then describes how he foolishly challenged the king of Israel (Yisrael) to a battle and was decisively defeated. Ultimately his officials conspired against him and killed him.

1. Introduction to the reign of Amaziah (1–2)
2. Amaziah obeys the law by executing only his father’s murderers (3–4)
3. Amaziah obeys Yahweh by sending back the mercenaries he had hired (5–10)
4. Amaziah defeates the Edomites but then worships their gods (11–16)
5. Amaziah challenges King Joash of Israel to a battle and is defeated (17–24)
6. Conclusion to the reign of Amaziah (25–28)

# 2 Chronicles 26 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the author’s account of the reign of Uzziah (Uziyah), Amaziah’s (Amatsyah’s) son. (Uzziah is called Azariah (Azaryah) in the parallel account of his reign in 2 Kings.) This chapter describes how Uzziah was at first a good king because of the influence of a prophet named Zechariah (Zekaryah) (not the same one whose prophecies are recorded in the biblical book of Zechariah). It relates how he defeated Judah’s (Yehudah’s) enemies and made his kingdom militarily powerful. But it then describes how he became proud and went into Yahweh’s temple to offer incense, trying to make himself a priest-king like the rulers of pagan nations. Yahweh punished him by making him a leper, so that he could no longer rule the kingdom and had to live in seclusion.

1. Introduction to the reign of Uzziah (1–5)
2. Uzziah’s military victories (6–8)
3. Uzziah’s military preparations (9–15)
4. Uzziah’s sin of offering incense in the temple and his punishment (16–21)
5. Conclusion to the reign of Uzziah (22–23)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Did Uzziah’s father Amaziah really “do right in the eyes of Yahweh”?

Readers may wonder how the author can say in 26:4 that Uzziah (Uziyah) “did right in the eyes of Yahweh, like all that Amaziah (Amatsyah) his father had done” when Amaziah worshiped idols, refused to obey a prophet’s warning, engaged in a disastrous military campaign, and was murdered by his officials because of his unfaithfulness to Yahweh. The answer is that the author is writing very precisely. He uses a standard formula that seems to mean “just as Amaziah his father had done.” (Compare the statement in 29:2 about Hezekiah (Hizkiyah), “he did right in the eyes of Yahweh, like all that David his father had done.”) But the author qualifies this in the next verse by saying that Uzziah “was seeking God in the days of Zechariah (Zekaryah)” and that “in the days of his seeking Yahweh, God made him prosper.” This makes the reader wonder what Uzziah did after Zechariah died. Later in the chapter, the author relates that after he became a powerful ruler, Uzziah “transgressed against Yahweh his God” (26:16). So the author means exactly what he says in verse 4. # 2 Chronicles 27 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the author’s account of the reign of Jotham (Yotam), Uzziah’s (Uziyah’s) son. It describes how he was a powerful king, victorious over his enemies, because he was loyal to Yahweh.

3. Conclusion to the reign of Jotham (7–9)

# 2 Chronicles 28 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the author’s account of the reign of Ahaz, Jotham’s (Yotam’s) son. It describes how he was a wicked king who worshiped idols and engaged in the same evil practices as the pagan nations whom Yahweh had enabled the Israelites (Israelis) to conquer and displace. The chapter relates how, as a result, Yahweh enabled various enemies to defeat the Judeans (Yehudim) and take many of their people captive. It describes how, in response, Ahaz appealed to the Assyrians for help and worshiped even more foreign gods, but this did not benefit him.

1. Introduction to the reign of Ahaz (1–4)
2. The Arameans and Israelites defeat Ahaz (5–8)
3. The prophet Oded makes the Israelites return the Judean (Yehudi) captives (9–15)
4. Ahaz asks the Assyrians for help and worships more idols but suffers further defeats (16–25)
3. Conclusion to the reign of Ahaz (26–27)

# 2 Chronicles 29 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the author’s account of the reign of Hezekiah (Hizkiyah), Ahaz’s son. It describes how he restored the worship of Yahweh in Judah (Yehudah) by having the priests and Levites clean out all the idolatrous material from the temple courtyards and building. It then tells how Hezekiah and the Judean (Yehudi) leaders held a special ceremony with many of the people to rededicate the temple.

1. Introduction to the reign of Hezekiah (1–2)
2. Hezekiah tells the priests and Levites to clean out the temple area (3–19)
3. Hezekiah and the Judean leaders rededicate the temple (20–36)

# 2 Chronicles 30 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of Hezekiah (Hizkiyah). It tells how he and the Judean (Yehudi) leaders held a Passover celebration in Jerusalem (Yerushalem) for all Israelites (Israelis), such as no other king had done since the reign of Solomon (Shelomoh).

1. Hezekiah and the princes agree to hold a Passover celebration (1–4)
2. The invitation to all Israelites from Hezekiah and the princes (5–12)
3. The Passover celebration (13–21)
4. The people celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread afterwards (22–25)
4. Conclusion to the account of this celebration (26–27)

# 2 Chronicles 31 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of Hezekiah (Hizkiyah). It tells how he arranged for the priests and Levites to receive regular support from the Judeans (Yehudim) so that they could devote themselves to their sacred duties.

1. Further conclusion to the Passover account (1)
2. Hezekiah provides for the priests and Levites and tells the Judeans to do the same (2–4)
3. The Judeans give so generously that the surplus must be stored in the temple (5–11)
4. The administrators and how they distributed to the priests and Levites (12–19)
5. Summary conclusion (20–21)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Why does the author say “the sons of Israel (Yisrael)” in 31:5 but “the sons of Israel and Judah (Yehudah)” in 31:6?

The phrase “the sons of Israel” in verse 5 is equivalent to the phrase “the dwellers of Jerusalem (Yerushalem)” in verse 4. The author is describing these people as Israelites (Israelis), even though they live in what is now the southern kingdom of Judah. However, in verse 6, the author speaks of “the sons of Israel and Judah, the dwellers in the cities of Judah.” Here he does seem to intend a distinction between people who had come from the northern kingdom to live in Judah and people who had been Judeans (Yehudim) all along. Readers may wonder why the author draws no such distinction in verse 5, since the inhabitants of Jerusalem presumably also included both groups. The subtle variation in phrasing seems to provide a glimpse into the chronicler’s theology. People who live in the city where Yahweh’s temple is and where David’s descendants still reign are the legitimate heirs of the Israelite (Israeli) monarchy. That is the spiritual reality. But away from the direct influence of the temple and the king, the historical reality is felt. The kingdom has been divided and many of the people of the southern kingdom have moved there from their traditional territories in the north. If possible, represent these phrases in your translation in a way that will allow your readers to appreciate the author’s purposes in using them.

# 2 Chronicles 32 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the author’s account of the reign of Hezekiah (Hizkiyah). It describes how the Assyrian emperor Sennacherib (Sanheriv) led a great army to invade Judah (Yehudah) and threaten Jerusalem (Yerushalem). It relates how Yahweh sent an angel who killed the Assyrian soldiers and how the emperor himself was killed when he returned to his land. The chapter then relates how Yahweh healed Hezekiah of a deadly illness, and it describes his wealth and projects.

1. The Assyrians invade Judah and Hezekiah encourages the people (1–8)
2. The Assyrian officers try to frighten and intimidate the people of Jerusalem (9–19)
3. Yahweh destroys the Assyrian army (20–23)
4. Yahweh heals Hezekiah of a deadly illness (24–26)
5. Hezekiah’s wealth and projects (27–31)
6. Conclusion to the reign of Hezekiah (32–33)

# 2 Chronicles 33 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the author’s accounts of the reigns of Manasseh (Menasheh), Hezekiah’s (Hizkiyah’s) son, and of Amon, Manasseh’s son. It describes how Manasseh was a wicked king who worshiped idols and, in ways even worse than Ahaz, engaged in the same evil practices as the pagan nations whom Yahweh had enabled the Israelites (Israelis) to conquer and displace. The chapter relates how, as a result, Yahweh enabled the Assyrians to conquer Manasseh’s kingdom and take him away as a prisoner. It describes how, in response, Manasseh repented and honored Yahweh as the true God, and how Yahweh returned him to his kingdom, where Manasseh then remained loyal to him. However, the chapter then relates how, after the death of Manasseh, his son Amon worshiped the same foreign idols that he had formerly worshiped. He was such a bad king that his officials murdered him.

1. Introduction to the reign of Manasseh (1–2)
2. The great wickedness and idolatry of Manasseh (3–10)
3. The Assyrians defeat and capture Manasseh, and he repents (11–17)
4. Conclusion to the reign of Manasseh (18–20)
5. The author’s account of the reign of Amon (21–25)

# 2 Chronicles 34 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the author’s account of the reign of Josiah (Yoshiyah), Amon’s son. It describes how destroyed the altars and idols of foreign gods throughout the territory of Israel (Yisrael). It then relates how he had the priests and Levites repair Yahweh’s temple. The chapter tells how a scroll of the law of Moses (Mosheh) was discovered during the temple repair work and how, when Josiah heard what it said, he sent officials seek a message from Yahweh about what would happen to the Judeans (Yehudim) because they had not the law. The officials went to the prophetess Huldah, who told them on behalf of Yahweh that the people would be punished but that Josiah himself would die before that happened. The chapter then describes how Josiah led the people of Judah (Yehudah) to renew their covenant with Yahweh.

1. Introduction to the reign of Josiah (1–2)
2. Josiah destroys the foreign altars and idols throughout Israel (3–7)
3. Josiah has the priests and Levites repair Yahweh’s temple (8–13)
4. The discovery of the scroll of the law (14–21)
5. Huldah’s response to Josiah’s officials (22–28)
6. Josiah leads the people to renew their covenant with Yahweh (29–33)

# 2 Chronicles 35 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the author’s account of the reign of Josiah (Yoshiyah). It describes how he held a great Passover celebration in Jerusalem (Yerushalem) for all of the surviving Israelites (Israelis) just as the law of Moses (Mosheh) instructed. It then relates how he led his army to oppose the Egyptian (Mitsri) king Neco (Nekoh) and was killed in battle against him.

1. Josiah summons the Israelites to Jerusalem to celebrate Passover (1–19)
2. Josiah opposes the Egyptian king Neco and is killed in battle (20–25)
3. Conclusion to the reign of Josiah (26–27)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did the Levites, not the people, slaughter the Passover animals?

The author says in verse 6 that Josiah told the Levites to slaughter the animals for the Passover festival, and he reports in verse 11 that they did this. Ordinarily, the worshiper would slaughter the animal for the sacrifice. But the Levites may have slaughtered them on behalf of the people for the same reason that the author gives in 30:17, “many were in the assembly who had not consecrated themselves, so the Levites were over the slaughtering of the Passovers for all who were not clean to consecrate them to Yahweh.” Perhaps in light of some memory or record of this experience during the reign of Hezekiah (Hizkiyah), Josiah told the Levites to consecrate themselves in advance of this festival. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain this in a footnote.

### How was Josiah’s (Yoshiyah’s) Passover the first of its kind since Samuel (Shmuel)?

Hezekiah had celebrated a Passover that the author says in 30:26 was the first of its kind since the reign of Solomon (Shelomoh). He says in 35:18 of Josiah’s celebration, “Now a Passover like it had not been made in Israel (Yisrael) from the days of Samuel the prophet.” Readers may wonder in what ways Josiah’s Passover was different from Hezekiah’s so as to be unprecedented to that degree. For one thing, Josiah celebrated Passover in the first month of the year, as the law specified, rather than in the second month, as Hezekiah had done out of necessity. Beyond that, the author does not say that Josiah had to intercede for people who ate the Passover without being ritually clean, as Hezekiah had had to do. The author also does not record any resistance from northerners, as he unfortunately has to do in the case of Hezekiah’s festival (30:10). The chronicler’s main point in 35:18 is probably that Josiah did “according to the word of Yahweh by the hand of Moses (Mosheh)” (v. 6), “as written in the scroll of Moses” (v. 12). In other words, his Passover was the most faithful to the instructions of the law since the time of Samuel. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain this in a footnote, particularly if they might otherwise wonder how 35:18 may be reconciled with 30:26.

# 2 Chronicles 36 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents the author’s account of the reigns of the last four kings of Judah (Yehudah): Jehoahaz (Yehoahaz), Jehoiakim (Yehoyakim), Jehoiachin (Yehoyakin), and Zedekiah (Tsidkiyah). All were sons of Josiah (Yoshiyah) except Jehoiachin, who was the son of Jehoiakim. These were bad, weak kings whom the Egyptians (Mitsrim) and Babylonians captured and exiled. Nebuchadnezzar (Nevukadnetsar) made Zedekiah his vassal, but when he rebelled, Nebuchadnezzar came and conquered Jerusalem (Yerushalem) and destroyed the temple and the city. However, the chapter, and the book, end on a hopeful note. The author quotes the beginning of the edict by the Persian emperor Cyrus (Koresh) that allowed the Judeans (Yehudim) to return home. This leads into the account of their return in the book of Ezra, which continues the story from where it ends here.

1. The reign of Jehoahaz (1–3)
2. The reign of Jehoiakim (4–8)
3. The reign of Jehoiachin (9–10)
4. The reign of Zedekiah (11–16)
5. The Babylonians destroy Jerusalem (17–21)
6. The Persian emperor Cyrus allows the Judeans to return home (22–23)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The royal proclamation by Cyrus (Koresh)

In verses 22–23, the author quotes, after an introduction, the beginning of the royal proclamation by Cyrus that allowed the Judeans (Yehudim) to return home. The full proclamation, with the same introduction, is in Ezra 1:1–4. This was a device by which ancient scribes showed that a document or story continued on another scroll. They would copy part of the continuation onto the end of the scroll that told the earlier part of the story. That is why 2 Chronicles 36:22–23 duplicates Ezra 1:1–2 but does not include the rest of the proclamation from Ezra 1:3–4. The result is that 2 Chronicles ends in mid-sentence (although this may not be clear to readers until they start the book of Ezra). 2 Chronicles ends, “Whoever among you is from all of his people, may Yahweh his God be with him, and may he go up …” The beginning of Ezra shows that the full sentence continues: “and may he go up to Jerusalem (Yerushalem), which is in Judah (Yehudah), and may he build the house of Yahweh, the God of Israel (Yisrael). He is the God who is in Jerusalem.” We do not recommend that you supply the rest of the proclamation in 2 Chronicles. But you may wish to inform readers in a footnote that only part of the proclamation is here and explain why that is so.

The author is using the participle **found**, which functions as an adjective in this context, as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and the thing found upon him] or [and what was found upon him]

The author is using the term **found** in a way characteristic of his language and culture to describe what could be found, that is, what was present in Jehoiakim’s (Yehoyakim’s) life. The implication in context is that this was something bad. See how you translated the comparable expression “good things have been found with you” in [19:3](../19/03.md). Alternate translation: [and the bad things that were present in his life]

Quote: בֶּן־שְׁמוֹנֶ֤ה שָׁנִים֙ יְהוֹיָכִ֣ין בְּ⁠מָלְכ֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁלֹשָׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ וַ⁠עֲשֶׂ֣רֶת יָמִ֔ים מָלַ֖ךְ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וַ⁠יַּ֥עַשׂ הָ⁠רַ֖ע בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֥י יְהוָֽה
Note: In this verse, the author is introducing **Jehoiachin (Yehoyakin)** as a participant in the story as the new king of Judah (Yehudah). If your language has its own way of introducing new participants, you could use it here in your translation.

The standard written Hebrew text as we have it today reads “eight.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “eighteen,” as in the parallel in [2 Kings 24:8](../../2ki/24/08.md). If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [eighteen]
See how you translated the same expression in [20:1](../20/01.md). Alternate translation: [at the start of the next year] or [the next spring]
**Zedekiah (Tsidkiyah)** was actually the brother of Jehoiachin’s (Yehoyakin’s) father. Your language may have its own term or expression for this relationship. Alternate translation: [his uncle]

Quote: בֶּן־עֶשְׂרִ֧ים וְ⁠אַחַ֛ת שָׁנָ֖ה צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ בְ⁠מָלְכ֑⁠וֹ וְ⁠אַחַ֤ת עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
Note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is introducing ** Zedekiah (Tsidkiyah) ** as a participant in the story as the new king of Judah (Yehudah). If your language has its own way of introducing new participants, you could use it here in your translation.

Here, **face** has the sense of opposing or confronting, as in contexts such as [12:5](../12/05.md) and [35:22](../35/22.md). Alternate translation: [when Jeremiah (Yirmiyah) Jeremiah the prophet confronted him]
See how you translated the similar expression “from the mouth of God” in [35:22](../35/22.md). Alternate translation: [, who spoke messages to him from Yahweh]
See how you translated the similar expression in [30:8](../30/08.md). Alternate translation: [And he resisted stubbornly]

The author is speaking as if Zedekiah’s (Tsidkiyah’s) **heart** had been a soft substance that he could have **hardened**. He is using the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts and desires. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable figure of speech or express the idea plainly. Alternate translation: [and he refused to consider the consequences of not turning]
See how you translated the similar expression in [25:27](../25/27.md). Alternate translation: [against worshiping Yahweh]

For emphasis, the author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [committed many very serious sins]

Quote: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֡ח יְהוָה֩ אֱלֹהֵ֨י אֲבוֹתֵי⁠הֶ֧ם עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם בְּ⁠יַ֥ד מַלְאָכָ֖י⁠ו הַשְׁכֵּ֣ם וְ⁠שָׁל֑וֹחַ כִּֽי־חָמַ֥ל עַל־עַמּ֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠עַל־מְעוֹנֽ⁠וֹ
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And because Yahweh, the God of their fathers, had compassion on his people and on his dwelling, he sent to them by the hand of his messengers, rising early and sending]

See how you translated the similar expression “by the hand of Moses (Mosheh)” in [35:6](../35/06.md). Alternate translation: [by the agency of his messengers] or [by sending them messages through his prophets]

The author is using **rising early** as a common expression of his culture to describe someone doing something continually. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [sending them all day long] or [sending them continually]

The author is using the term **words** to represent what Yahweh said through his prophets by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what he said through them]
See how you translated the similar expression in [34:21](../34/21.md). Alternate translation: [until Yahweh became very angry with his people]

See how you translated the similar expression “he healed the people” in [30:20](../30/20.md), where it probably means “he did not punish the people.” Alternate translation: [until he had to punish them]

Quote: וַ⁠יַּ֨עַל עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֜ם אֶת־מֶ֣לֶךְ כשדיים וַ⁠יַּהֲרֹ֨ג בַּחוּרֵי⁠הֶ֤ם בַּ⁠חֶ֨רֶב֙ בְּ⁠בֵ֣ית מִקְדָּשָׁ֔⁠ם וְ⁠לֹ֥א חָמַ֛ל עַל־בָּח֥וּר וּ⁠בְתוּלָ֖ה זָקֵ֣ן וְ⁠יָשֵׁ֑שׁ הַ⁠כֹּ֖ל נָתַ֥ן בְּ⁠יָדֽ⁠וֹ
Note: In the first and fourth instances, the pronoun “he” refers to Yahweh. In the second and third instances, it refers to the **king of the Chaldeans (Kasdim)**, as does the pronoun **his**. The author is using the king to represent his entire army. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh brought up the king of the Chaldeans against them, and the king killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary, and the king did not pity a young man or a virgin, old or grey-haired. Yahweh gave all into the king’s hand]
See how you translated the similar expression in verse 6. Alternate translation: [And he influenced the king of the Chaldeans (Kasdim) to attack them]

The term **Chaldeans (Kasdim)** is another name for the people group also known as Babylonians. If you have decided to use the same names in your translation that the biblical author does in each place, you may wish to use the name Chaldeans here. If you have decided to use the same names for people and groups throughout your translation, you may wish to use the name Babylonians here. Alternate translation: [the Babylonians]

The author is not referring to a specific **swords**. He means the swords in general of the Babylonian soldiers. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and his soldiers killed their young men with their swords]

In this context, the term **house** seems refer to the temple building, and the term **young men** seems to refer to able-bodied soldiers. The implication is that some of the Judean (Yehudi) soldiers sought refuge in the temple area, apparently within the temple building itself. While this would ordinarily have been a safe place or **sanctuary** for them (the author seems to be using that word in two senses, a “holy place” and a “safe place”), the Babylonians did not respect this cultural practice and they killed the soldiers who had sought refuge in the temple. Alternate translation: [, even those who sought refuge inside the temple building]

Quote: וְ⁠לֹ֥א חָמַ֛ל עַל־בָּח֥וּר וּ⁠בְתוּלָ֖ה זָקֵ֣ן וְ⁠יָשֵׁ֑שׁ
Note: The author is referring to the entire Judean (Yehudi) population by naming two kinds of major components, (1) male and female and (2) young and old. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. The UST models one way to do that.

Here, the **hand** of a person represents his power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into his power]

The author is referring to the entire collection of **vessels** in the temple by naming two extremes, **great** and **small**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every last one of them] or [without exception]

Here, the **sword** represents being killed, since the Babylonian soldiers used their swords to kill the Judeans (Yehudim). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the remnant who remained alive]

The author is using the term **sons** to mean “descendants” and specifically the descendants of Nebuchadnezzar (Nevukadnetsar) who ruled Babylon (Bavel) as kings after him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his successors]

The author is speaking of the **kingdom of Persia (Paras)** as if it had been a living thing that could have been able to **reign**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the kingdom of Persia replaced the Babylonian kingdom]

To translate this expression and the similar one in the next verse, see how you translated the similar expressions in verses 12 and 16. Alternate translation: [the message from Yahweh that Jeremiah (Yirmiyah) had spoken]

The author is speaking of the **land** of Israel (Yisrael) as if it had been a living thing that could have **enjoyed its Sabbaths** and **rested**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. The UST models one way to do that.

The author is using the term **days** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the whole time of its being desolated]

The expression **being desolated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for the whole time that it was desolate] or [for the whole time that no one lived there]

If, in such a context, your language would not represent a number in a form such as **18**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [And in the first year of the reign of Cyrus (Koresh)]

The author is speaking as if the **spirit** of Cyrus (Koresh) had actually been asleep and Yahweh **awakened** it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in [21:16](../21/16.md). Alternate translation: [And Yahweh influenced Cyrus]

The author is speaking of a **voice** as if it were a living thing that Cyrus (Koresh) could have made **pass through** the territory of his kingdom. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in [30:5](../30/05.md). Alternate translation: [and he spread the word] or [and he had messengers make a proclamation]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he also sent out written copies of his proclamation]

Quote: כֹּה־אָמַ֞ר כּ֣וֹרֶשׁ ׀ מֶ֣לֶךְ פָּרַ֗ס כָּל־מַמְלְכ֤וֹת הָ⁠אָ֨רֶץ֙ נָ֣תַן לִ֗⁠י יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֔יִם וְ⁠הֽוּא־פָקַ֤ד עָלַ⁠י֙ לִ⁠בְנֽוֹת־ל֣⁠וֹ בַ֔יִת בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֣ר בִּֽ⁠יהוּדָ֑ה מִֽי־בָ⁠כֶ֣ם מִ⁠כָּל־עַמּ֗⁠וֹ יְהוָ֧ה אֱלֹהָ֛י⁠ו עִמּ֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠יָֽעַל
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Cyrus (Koresh), the king of Persia (Paras), says that Yahweh, the God of the heavens, has given all of the kingdoms of the earth to him. And he, he has appointed him to build a house for him in Jerusalem (Yerushalem), which is in Judah (Yehudah). Cyrus says that whoever among you is from all of his people, may Yahweh his God be with him, and let him go up]

Cyrus (Koresh) is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. However, since an overstatement like this one was typical of a ruler in this culture, you may wish to retain the overstatement in your translation. It might not seem realistic or accurate to have Cyrus say something such as “has enable me to conquer many kingdoms in this area.”

Cyrus (Koresh) is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he has appointed** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize Yahweh’s personal role in appointing him to build a temple for him. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And he has personally appointed me to build a temple for him in Jerusalem (Yerushalem)]

Cyrus (Koresh) is using the term **all** to mean that people from any Israelite (Israeli) tribe may return to Judah (Yehudah). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [is from any of the Israelite tribes]
See how you translated the similar expression in [1:1](../01/01.md). Alternate translation: [may Yahweh his God help him]
Cyrus (Koresh) is marking travel for change in elevation. See how you translated the similar expression “David had brought up” in [1:4](../01/04.md). Alternate translation: [and let him return there]
